analysis.one_liner: Lets the post office offer cheap small-dollar loans, savings accounts, check cashing, and money transfers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate's final days of 2024 and sent to committee, the Postal Banking Act died with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the U.S. Postal Service offer basic banking at its roughly 30,000 locations: small loans up to $500 (up to $1,000 in a year) with the interest rate capped near the Treasury's borrowing rate, checking and savings accounts holding up to $20,000, check cashing, bill pay, debit cards, and domestic and international money transfers. It explicitly bars USPS from partnering with private banks, and directs the Federal Reserve to supply whatever funding is needed so the products sharply reduce the number of people without bank accounts. The bill was introduced on December 19, 2024, the last week of a dying Congress, and was never taken up by its committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly one in twenty U.S. households without a bank account, plus low- and moderate-income people who rely on payday loans, check-cashing stores, and high-fee money transfers. They would gain access to a $500 loan at roughly the government's own borrowing rate instead of triple-digit payday fees, a savings account paying at least the standard national rate, and cheap remittances.

how_it_helps.text: Directs USPS to make small-dollar loans of up to $500 at a time ($1,000 within a year of a first loan), with total interest and fees capped at 101 percent of the one-month Treasury rate — a fraction of payday-loan costs.
Requires savings accounts to pay at least the national average rate on savings and allows accounts up to $20,000, giving people outside the banking system a safe place to keep money.
Adds check cashing, debit cards, bill pay, mobile banking, and domestic and foreign money transfers at post offices, replacing fee-heavy private alternatives.

Orders the Federal Reserve to transfer funds sufficient to make these products substantially reduce the number of unbanked people and users of payday loans, check cashing, prepaid cards, and overdraft fees.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, check-cashing stores, and money-transfer companies lose a captive market of high-fee customers. Banks are also locked out: the bill forbids USPS from offering these services through partnerships with private institutions. If the program runs deficits, funding comes through Federal Reserve transfers, spreading any cost across the public.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders, check cashers, remittance firms, banks

drawbacks.text: USPS would take on lending risk in a business it has never run; the bill covers the program through Federal Reserve transfers, so loan losses and shortfalls would fall on public funds rather than a private balance sheet.
Loans are capped at $500 at a time and $1,000 in a year, which covers emergency gaps but is small next to what many payday borrowers need, limiting how much of the market it can replace.

The bill bans any partnership with banks or credit unions, so USPS must build accounts, payments, and lending from scratch rather than piggybacking on institutions that already have some small-dollar loan experience.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it targets, the benefit is large and direct: near-zero-interest small-dollar credit and basic accounts where payday lenders and check cashers currently charge the most. The honest costs are that a government agency with no lending track record would absorb credit risk with public backing, the loan ceilings are modest, and banks are deliberately excluded. Whether the program is well run would decide whether those costs matter; the design gives regulators (Treasury, the consumer bureau, banking agencies) a role in writing the rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with two weeks left in the Congress, referred to the Senate Homeland Security committee, and died there when the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Postal Banking Act on December 19, 2024, with Sen. Bernie Sanders as the bill's sole cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day.
No further action of any kind was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, leaving the bill dead in committee.
The bill text directs the Federal Reserve to transfer funding sufficient to substantially reduce the number of unbanked Americans and users of payday lending and check cashing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders, check-cashing stores, and remittance companies keep their customers and fees. People without bank accounts continue paying those costs. Postal banking also stays off the books, so banks keep the field to themselves.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Postal Banking Act on December 19, 2024.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: Payday lending and check-cashing industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed postal banking proposals that would put near-zero-cost small-dollar loans and check cashing in direct competition with its products.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Independent cosponsor and no Republican support; it never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists.

industries.note: The bill would let the post office make $500 loans at an interest rate pegged near the Treasury rate and cash checks, directly undercutting products that often carry triple-digit annual costs for the same customers. Their gain depends on those customers having no cheaper option.
USPS would offer domestic and international remittances, competing with high-fee wire and transfer services used heavily by immigrants sending money home.

The bill explicitly bars USPS from offering any of these services through partnerships with insured depository institutions, so banks are cut out of a new financial channel — they lose potential deposits and accounts to a $20,000-capped postal account, though most never offered these products to unbanked customers anyway.
USPS gains a new revenue-generating service line backed by Federal Reserve funding, and a clearer public-interest mission serving customers banks decline to serve.
